title: Dengue: assessment and fluid management (WHO)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Recognise warning signs and admit. Protocolised oral fluids and paracetamol (or metamizole) for non-severe disease, never NSAIDs or steroids. Severe disease: isotonic crystalloid rather than colloid, titrated by capillary refill time, lactate and haematocrit, tapered and stopped within 48 hours; no prophylactic platelets.

sections.title: Recognise and classify
items: Febrile phase 2 to 7 days. The critical phase of plasma leakage starts around defervescence (day 4 to 6) and usually settles within 48 to 72 hours, followed by reabsorption of fluid in the recovery phase.

Warning signs: progressive or sustained abdominal pain, persistent vomiting (3 or more episodes in 1 hour or 4 in 6 hours), lethargy, irritability or drowsiness, mucosal bleeding, liver more than 2 cm below the costal margin, clinical fluid accumulation, and a haematocrit rising on 2 consecutive measurements.

Severe dengue (WHO 2009): plasma leakage causing shock or fluid accumulation with respiratory distress; severe bleeding; or severe organ involvement (AST or ALT 1000 U/L or more, impaired consciousness, heart or other organs).
Compensated shock precedes hypotension: tachycardia, cold peripheries, capillary refill above 3 seconds on the WHO standardised method, and a narrowing pulse pressure (20 mmHg or less).

Admit (WHO 2025): warning signs, severe dengue, oral intolerance, difficulty breathing, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension, AKI, prolonged capillary refill, pregnancy or coagulopathy. Consider admission at the extremes of age and with significant comorbidity or poor social support.
Tests: NS1 antigen, RT-PCR or rapid antigen tests in the first week; IgM from the end of the first week (cross-reacts with Zika). CBC with haematocrit and platelets as a baseline and serially.

sections.title: Non-severe dengue (outpatient)
items: Protocolised oral fluids: give a measured cup and ask the patient or carer to record intake daily; ORS preferred, with water, soups, coconut water or rice water. Aim to pass urine 4 to 6 times a day. Avoid carbonated or sweetened drinks above 5% sugar.

Paracetamol for fever or pain: adults over 50 kg 500 mg to 1 g every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 g/day); children 10 to 15 mg/kg every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 60 mg/kg/day); not more often than 4-hourly. Use with caution in liver disease or transaminitis.
Metamizole is an alternative where available (adults 500 mg to 1 g, children 10 mg/kg per dose, up to 4 times daily); warn about agranulocytosis and avoid in the third trimester and breastfeeding.
Do not give NSAIDs, including aspirin (WHO strong recommendation), or corticosteroids. Avoid intramuscular injections.

Review daily from day 3 of illness until out of the critical phase (symptoms, warning signs, urine frequency, CBC and haematocrit). Tell patients to return at once with any warning sign or no urine for 4 to 6 hours.

sections.title: Warning signs without shock (admit)
items: Take a reference haematocrit before IV fluids. Give isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline, Ringer lactate or Hartmann) 5 to 7 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours, then 3 to 5 mL/kg/h for 2 to 4 hours, then 2 to 3 mL/kg/h or less according to response.

Reassess and repeat the haematocrit. If it is unchanged or rising only minimally, continue 2 to 3 mL/kg/h for another 2 to 4 hours. If vital signs worsen and haematocrit rises rapidly, increase to 5 to 10 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours and reassess.
Give the minimum volume that maintains good perfusion and a urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h. Calculate rates on ideal body weight in obesity.
Patients with comorbidity but no warning signs: encourage oral fluids; if not tolerated, IV isotonic fluid at maintenance rate, reviewed frequently.
IV fluids are usually needed for only 24 to 48 hours; taper as leakage stops.

sections.title: Dengue shock
items: Use isotonic crystalloid rather than colloid (WHO 2025). Obtain a reference haematocrit, group and cross-match, and guide every step by capillary refill time and lactate as well as pulse, BP, pulse pressure, urine output and haematocrit.

Compensated shock: crystalloid 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over 1 hour in adults (10 to 20 mL/kg/h over 1 hour in infants and children). If improving, adults 5 to 7 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours, 3 to 5 mL/kg/h for 2 to 4 hours, then 2 to 3 mL/kg/h; children 10, then 7, then 5, then 3 mL/kg/h.
Hypotensive shock (all ages): 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 to 30 minutes. If improving, 10 mL/kg/h for 1 hour, then taper stepwise as for compensated shock.

Shock persists with haematocrit still high or rising: a further bolus of 10 to 20 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes, then 7 to 10 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours once improving. Use a passive leg raise test when unsure whether more fluid will help (a rise in cardiac output above 10% predicts response).

Shock persists with haematocrit falling or inappropriately normal (for example below 40 to 45% in adult men, 35 to 40% in women and children): suspect occult bleeding and transfuse fresh packed red cells 5 to 10 mL/kg or fresh whole blood 10 to 20 mL/kg.

Refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg: look for bleeding, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, myocardial dysfunction and bacterial sepsis; ICU for vasoactive support. Total IV fluid should not exceed 48 hours.

sections.title: Monitoring and when to stop fluids
items: Warning signs: vital signs and perfusion 1 to 4-hourly until out of the critical phase, urine output 4 to 6-hourly, haematocrit before and after fluid changes then 6 to 12-hourly, plus glucose, renal, liver and coagulation tests as indicated.

Shock: continuous observation, hourly urine output (aim 0.5 mL/kg/h or more), capillary refill time with each reassessment, and lactate every 2 to 4 hours while it is guiding resuscitation (unreliable in liver failure).

Reduce or stop IV fluids when leakage stops: stable BP, pulse and perfusion; haematocrit falling with a good pulse volume; afebrile 24 to 48 hours without antipyretics; resolving abdominal symptoms; improving urine output.
Fluid beyond 48 hours of the critical phase causes pulmonary oedema; a falling haematocrit with stable circulation in recovery means haemodilution, not a need for more fluid.

sections.title: Bleeding, platelets and fluid overload
items: Do not give prophylactic platelets for counts below 50,000/microlitre without active bleeding (WHO 2025). Platelets may be considered before surgery or invasive procedures, or with pre-existing anticoagulation.

Severe bleeding: control the source where possible and transfuse fresh packed red cells 5 to 10 mL/kg or fresh whole blood 10 to 20 mL/kg without waiting for the haematocrit to fall far; a haematocrit trigger of 30% is not valid in dengue. Check PT, APTT and fibrinogen.

Fluid overload (respiratory distress, rising respiratory rate, large effusions, tense ascites): give oxygen; out of the critical phase with warm peripheries, stop IV fluids and give furosemide 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg per dose 2 to 3 times daily or 0.1 mg/kg/h by infusion, watching potassium.
Still within the critical phase and stable: reduce IV fluids and avoid diuretics, which can precipitate intravascular depletion.
No systemic corticosteroids or immunoglobulins in severe dengue (WHO 2025).

sections.title: Pregnancy, infants and comorbidity
items: Pregnancy is an admission criterion. Physiological haemodilution lowers the baseline haematocrit and fluid tolerance is narrow; involve obstetrics and observe the newborn if delivery occurs near maternal illness.
Infants and young children decompensate quickly; use the paediatric fluid rates above and paediatric paracetamol dosing.
Heart failure, CKD, elderly and obese patients: smaller aliquots, ideal body weight, and early senior review; judge hypotension against the patient's own baseline BP.

India: the NCVBDC 2023 guideline uses similar haematocrit-guided stepwise regimens but different starting rates, allows colloid for refractory leak and platelets below 10,000/mm3; this protocol follows WHO 2025 (crystalloid, no prophylactic platelets).

sections.title: Admission and discharge
items: Manage severe dengue in a hospital with blood transfusion facilities; refractory or decompensated shock, respiratory distress or organ failure needs ICU.
Discharge when all are present: no fever for 48 hours, clinical improvement, rising platelet trend, no respiratory distress, and a stable haematocrit without IV fluids (WHO 2012 handbook).
Outpatients must be able to drink adequately and pass urine at least every 6 hours, with a daily review arranged through the critical phase.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Discharging at defervescence, when the critical phase begins.
Treating the platelet count rather than perfusion and haematocrit.
Continuing IV fluids into the recovery phase, causing pulmonary oedema.
Missing concealed bleeding when shock persists with a falling or normal haematocrit.
Giving NSAIDs, aspirin, steroids or IM injections for fever and body ache.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: Adults over 50 kg 500 mg to 1 g every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 g/day; children 10 to 15 mg/kg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 60 mg/kg/day
drugs.notes: Not more often than 4-hourly; count all paracetamol sources. Caution with liver involvement.

drugs.name: Metamizole (dipyrone)
drugs.dose: Adults 500 mg to 1 g per dose (maximum 4 g/day); children 10 mg/kg per dose up to 4 times daily
drugs.notes: Alternative to paracetamol where licensed. Agranulocytosis risk; avoid in third trimester and breastfeeding.

drugs.name: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline, Ringer lactate, Hartmann)
drugs.dose: Warning signs: 5 to 7 mL/kg/h, tapering. Compensated shock: 5 to 10 mL/kg/h in adults, 10 to 20 mL/kg/h in children, over 1 hour. Hypotensive shock: 20 mL/kg over 15 to 30 minutes
drugs.notes: Taper stepwise by response; stop within 24 to 48 hours. Ideal body weight in obesity.

drugs.name: Packed red cells or whole blood
drugs.dose: Fresh packed red cells 5 to 10 mL/kg or fresh whole blood 10 to 20 mL/kg per aliquot
drugs.notes: Suspected or overt severe bleeding, or shock with falling haematocrit.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.dose: 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg per dose IV 2 to 3 times daily, or 0.1 mg/kg/h infusion
drugs.notes: Fluid overload once out of the critical phase and haemodynamically stable. Monitor potassium.
